newsitem.title: GERMANY: Krupp board meets, reviews Thyssen strategy.
newsitem.headline: Krupp board meets, reviews Thyssen strategy.

text.p: The supervisory board of German steel group Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp met on Saturday to discuss its strategy on talks with rival Thyssen AG and whether to relaunch a hostile takeover bid.
The extraordinary board meeting at Krupp's offices in Essen was called by board employee representatives who were to be given a briefing on Krupp's intentions.
The meeting took place as Germany's Die Welt newspaper reported on Saturday that Krupp plans to relaunch a hostile takeover bid for Thyssen as soon as the first week of April.

Citing reliable sources, the newspaper said Krupp believed Thyssen had only agreed to talks this week about a merger of their steel companies in order to win time to defend itself against a complete takeover. The talks began on Thursday and were also held on Friday at a secret location.
"But Krupp wants a complete merger," the newspaper wrote.
Krupp launched a rare hostile takeover of larger Thyssen earlier last week, offering shareholders 435 marks a share, a 25 percent premium over the previous day's share price.

The move sparked spontaneous work stoppages by thousands of steel workers in the Ruhr valley industrial heartland and local politicians intervened, persuading the two companies to begin talks over a merger of just their steel companies.

Also on Saturday, Germany's Focus magazine said a top Deutsche Bank AG official did not rule out resigning from the Thyssen supervisory board after trade unions sharply criticised Deutsche and Dresdner Bank for their role in the takeover.

"I will not rule out that I will give up my mandate at the end of the meeting (on Thursday)," Ulrich Cartellieri, who represents Deutsche's shareholder interests on the Thyssen board, told the magazine in an interview.

Walter Riester, the vice president of union IG Metall and also the deputy chairman of Thyssen's supervisory board, called on Friday for representatives from the two banks who are on the Thyssen and Krupp boards to quit due to the roles of their banks in the takeover.

A merger between Krupp and Thyssen would create one of the world's largest steel operations, but Krupp has said the full merger of the two companies would create cost savings in other areas as well, such as engineering and automotive components.
Citing consultant sources, the Die Welt report said Krupp expects annual savings of at least one billion marks in the event of complete merger with Thyssen.
According to the newspaper report, Krupp has secured sufficient bank financing for its offer and to counter potential defensive tactics by Thyssen.
One such move could be a decision by Thyssen to carry out an already-approved capital increase of 350 million marks. That would raise the costs for Krupp by around three billion marks.
Krupp has secured bank financing of 15 billion marks in the event that it has to acquire 100 percent of Thyssen's capital.

Die Welt said Krupp's steel merger plan would convert its traditional blast furnace operations in Dortmund to a modern electric steel plant, thereby cutting 1,500 jobs. But these job cuts would be carried out without layoffs.
